newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND'S ECONOMY IS KEY TO ITS EU ENTRY - PRESIDENT.
newsitem.headline: POLAND'S ECONOMY IS KEY TO ITS EU ENTRY - PRESIDENT.

text.p: Poland's economic performance in coming years is the key element in its drive to quickly join the European Union, President Aleksander Kwasniewski told Rzeczpospolita daily in an interview published on Saturday.

Kwasniewski said that since 1993, when the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) won parliamentary elections, Poland had drawn much closer to EU membership, but it could still spoil its success with unsound economic moves.

"Both the Czechs and the Poles are now treated as partners to start (EU accession) negotiations on January 1, 1998. But... it is 80 percent up to us and depends on what economic reforms will be made," Kwasniewski said.
"Poland is now closer to the EU than ever. But we can spoil that...if we make some strange economic decisions, if, for example, inflation starts to rise," he said.

Year-on-year inflation in October was at 19.5 percent, flat from September and down from 21.6 percent in December 1995. The government expects it will fall to 17.9-18.2 percent at the end of this year and drop to 13 percent in December 1997.
Kwasniewski said he hoped Poland would begin or continue the privatisation of its telecommunications, energy and banking sectors and sell off the KGHM copper concern.
"For me the key is for Poland to maintain high, and I want to stress 'high', economic growth. The second thing is to keep the budget deficit falling and the third is inflation," he said.
Poland's economy grew seven percent in 1995 and is expected to grow by 5.5 percent this year, and analysts expect the growth to continue at around five percent annually for the next two years.

Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, said he would not directly engage in the 1997 parliamentary election campaign but would point out programmes which provided new chances and those which posed threats to the country's main policy goals.
Warsaw, which threw off communism and Soviet domination in 1989, is pressing to join the EU and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as fast as possible.

"Nothing should be done to slow economic growth. Nothing should happen which would make our joining NATO more difficult and here the question of political stability and style in politics is very important. Also nothing should be done to disrupt our drive to the European Union," he said.
